added_claim_errors: Adds a 3.6% COLA to her statement figure as if certain ($2,486 at 67, $1,750 at 62). The key lists this as a side-claim trap, and the 2027 figure should be about $1,690.

Says she will be about $470 a month behind for life after the recompute at 67. My own rough recalculation, with about 20 withheld months credited, gives about $528, so this is unverifiable and probably low.
Break-even around age 78, about $63,000 received by 67, and waiting worth well over $50,000 in lifetime benefits. All are unverifiable and rest on the COLA-inflated $1,750.
Cites POMS RS 00615.015, an ecfr.io link for 20 CFR 404.410, and an ssa.gov 2027 factsheet URL. I did not open any of them, so none can be confirmed as supporting the exact claims.

Does not state that up to 85% of benefits may be taxable, although the $3,094 federal tax figure implicitly uses it. I recomputed the $3,094, the $2,907 FICA figure and the $3,250 net, and they are internally consistent.
Says she is first eligible for March 2027 and should file for March 2027 by applying around November 2026. This is wrong: she is first 62 for a whole month in April 2027, so benefits start in April.
Uses 36 plus 24 months, which is 60 months and a flat 30%. The correct count is 59 months early and a 29.58% reduction. The key accepts the $1,680 approximation, but the March start premise is wrong.
Says only about 9 payments land in 2027, roughly $9,000-$10,500 of Social Security cash. This is wrong: with whole-check withholding the figure is about $6,760-$7,000.

The budget table spreads the withholding as -$518 a month and a net $1,162 a month steady state. This misrepresents the 2027 cash flow, where whole checks are withheld and little or nothing arrives until about September.

The link text reads 'SSA's 2027 COLA and earnings-limit announcement' but the URL is adasoutheast.org, not SSA. The source is mislabeled and I did not open it to confirm it supports the $25,560 figure.
Federal tax of about $313 a month is an estimate with no stated assumptions. It only fits a full year of benefits, not 2027.

reasons: Both answers catch the two false premises at the start: the early-claiming reduction is permanent despite 40 years of work, and the earnings test applies. Both also get the 2027 earnings test right: $25,560 limit, $12,440 excess and $6,220 withheld. Answer A gets the April 2027 start, 59 months and 70.4% right, and its 2027 budget lands at about four payments and $7,000 of Social Security, which matches the key's timing of little until about September. A's weaknesses are applying a 3.6% COLA as certain, which gives $1,750 instead of about $1,690 and inflates its later break-even figures, and it is long with an unrequested claiming-age table. Answer B falls into the March-start trap (it also says to file for March 2027), and its 'steady-state' budget smooths the withholding. It also states a wrong 2027 cash figure of $9,000-$10,500 and links an ADA Southeast page labeled as SSA. B does mention 85% taxability and the check drought. Neither mentions the first-year monthly rule or checking with SSA's calculators or my Social Security. A's budget is more accurate for the year she asked about.
